challenge.alternative: The mechanism is the ACL Native Sparse Attention architecture or an unmodified dense MLA kernel.
challenge.check: Compare the first-party DSA paper's equations/Figure 1 and released configuration/model path with both alternatives.
challenge.outcome: The paper names DeepSeek Sparse Attention, gives a learned lightning indexer plus top-k token selection, instantiates it under MLA's MQA mode, and the release fixes index_topk=2048.

claims.claim: DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp introduces DeepSeek Sparse Attention with a lightning indexer and fine-grained top-k token selection, instantiates it under MLA's MQA mode, and its released 671B configuration selects 2048 entries per query.

evidence.observation: The first-party report defines both components and the MLA/MQA instantiation.
The released configuration sets 2048.

claims.claim: The two-stage pipeline reduces total per-query decode attention computation from O(sequence length) to O(topk=2048).

evidence.observation: Only core/main attention becomes O(Lk) over a sequence; the lightning indexer remains O(L squared), or O(L) work for one decode query, so the whole two-stage per-query path is not O(k).

claims.claim: The architecture diagram is an accurate general kernel contract: a 64-head/128-dimensional FP8 indexer with a 64-token page selects 2048 block indices, then a 16-head sparse MLA gathers them from one shared cache.

evidence.observation: The model has 64x128 indexer heads, 128 MLA query heads, latent 512 and RoPE 64; 16 MLA heads is only an eight-way local shard, not the architecture contract.
The indexer maintains a separate 128-dimensional FP8 K cache and scale cache, then emits token positions; MLA maintains separate latent and positional caches.
Decode indices encode selected token positions as physical-page-plus-offset values; they are not one index per KV block.

claims.claim: Every sparse-MLA KV cache entry is universally 656 bytes with 512 FP8 bytes, 16 bytes of per-block FP32 scales, 128 BF16 bytes for indexer positional encoding, and FlashMLA requires a fixed page size of 64.

evidence.observation: 656 bytes applies to that decode mode: 512 E4M3 NoPE values, four FP32 scales for successive 128-value groups, and 64 BF16 RoPE values for attention.
The official tests cover page sizes 2, 53, 61, 64, 69, 256 and 576, refuting a FlashMLA-wide fixed-64 requirement.
Indexer K storage is separate from the 656-byte attention cache.

claims.claim: The displayed lightning-indexer CUDA sketch accurately computes one maximum score per KV block using FP8 block-scale MMA and then runs top-k over blocks.

evidence.observation: The index score is per preceding token and is a weighted sum across indexer heads of ReLU-applied dot products, not a per-block maximum.

The reference forms q/k, applies non-interleaved RoPE and rotations, quantizes FP8, computes token logits, masks them, and calls topk over token positions; it does not implement the displayed signature or block-max reduction.
The high-performance kernel emits logits for Q-head/KV ranges using explicit weights and scales; top-k selection is outside this kernel.

claims.claim: The displayed sparse-decode CUDA sketch accurately takes 2048 selected block indices, a generic FP8 paged cache and a [16,576] query, gathers blocks, and runs standard MLA.

evidence.observation: The real interface accepts q[batch,s_q,h_q,576], the V3-family 656-byte FP8+sparse cache, and indices[batch,s_q,topk] whose values encode token page+offset; head count and topk are shape parameters, not the invented fixed signature.
The reference gathers token rows selected by encoded indices, applies attention across query heads, and masks invalid entries; it does not interpret each index as a selected block.

claims.claim: One H800 dense-MLA decode operating point simultaneously reaches 660 BF16 TFLOPS and 3000 GB/s and is compute-bound.

evidence.observation: The author reports separate maxima for memory-bound and compute-bound configurations; the row merges them into one operating point and label.

claims.claim: Sparse MLA decode on H800 performs FP8 matrix multiplication at 410 TFLOPS.

evidence.observation: The 410-TFLOPS author report is for H800 SXM5/CUDA 12.8, but only KV storage is FP8; the matrix multiplication is explicitly BF16.

claims.claim: Sparse MLA decode on B200 performs FP8 matrix multiplication at 350 TFLOPS and is lower than H800 because decode is bandwidth-dominated.

evidence.observation: The source says up to 350 TFLOPS and not really optimized yet; it specifies BF16 MMA over an FP8 cache and does not attribute the cross-GPU difference to bandwidth.

claims.claim: Dense MLA prefill reaches 1460 BF16 TFLOPS on B200 through tcgen05.

evidence.locator: dense prefill support matrix and performance
evidence.observation: The 1460 author-reported value belongs to NVIDIA's dense MHA forward implementation on SM100, not a dense MLA/MQA prefill result; the README does not label it tcgen05 peak.

claims.claim: Sparse MLA prefill on B200 is FP8, reaches 1450 TFLOPS, and therefore matches BF16 dense prefill.

evidence.locator: sparse MLA prefill performance and equivalent code
evidence.observation: The 1450 maximum on B200/CUDA 12.9 is author-reported, but the sparse-prefill Q/KV interface is BF16 and the source makes no matched-performance equivalence to the separate dense-MHA maximum.

claims.claim: Sparse MLA has a verified use threshold at context lengths of 32K or greater.

evidence.observation: The report presents H800 cost curves from 0K to 128K and even uses masked MHA for short prefill, but defines no universal 32K crossover or use threshold.

challenge.alternative: The released DSA kernels are unrelated to the DeepSeek-V3.2 model.
challenge.check: Follow the model repository's high-performance-kernel links and FlashMLA's release statement.
challenge.outcome: Both first-party repositories explicitly connect the indexer logits and sparse attention kernels to DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp DSA.

claims.claim: DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp is a directly supported use of the released indexer and FlashMLA sparse-attention kernels.

evidence.observation: The release links indexer logits to DeepGEMM and sparse attention to FlashMLA.
The repository says the sparse kernels power DSA in DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp.

claims.claim: The same sparse-kernel path can be recommended for unspecified similar MLA architectures.

evidence.observation: The APIs impose exact head dimensions, cache layout, dtype, head-count, index-shape, and output contracts; architectural similarity alone does not establish compatibility.

challenge.alternative: Sparse decode cannot affect per-token latency because the indexer still scans the prefix.
challenge.check: Compare the main-attention complexity reduction and first-party H800 service cost curve with the retained caveat about the indexer.
challenge.outcome: The main attention reads and computes over selected entries and the first-party deployment reports long-context end-to-end savings, supporting relevance but not universal superiority.

claims.claim: The DSA/FlashMLA path is relevant to serving measurements where long-context per-token decode latency matters, provided indexer and sparse-attention time are both included.

evidence.observation: The paper reports reduced H800 service costs in long-context decoding while retaining the indexer's complexity.
The attention kernel consumes selected-token indices and therefore addresses the selected-attention portion of decode.

claims.claim: A structured B200 performance record establishes 1450 FP8 TFLOPS for sparse prefill at sequence length 32K and topk 2048 and classifies it FP8 sparse compute-bound.

evidence.locator: sparse MLA prefill performance and API
evidence.observation: The source reports only up to 1450 TFLOPS on B200/CUDA 12.9; the inputs are BF16 and it supplies no 32K/topk-2048 tuple, compute-bound classification, timed region, repetitions, or variance.

claims.claim: SM100 tcgen05 FP8 block-scale MMA is the common mechanism enabling both the lightning indexer and sparse-attention stages.

evidence.observation: The indexer logit kernel uses FP8 UMMA with explicit Q/K scale handling, not the page's claimed shared FP8 block-scale attention pipeline.

evidence.locator: sparse decode and prefill dtype contracts
evidence.observation: Sparse decode dequantizes FP8 KV to BF16 for MMA; sparse prefill accepts BF16 Q/KV. SM100 source uses tcgen05/TMEM, but not one FP8 block-scale MMA mechanism for both stages.
